candidates.title: The AI buildout rests on hidden debt
candidates.why: How data centres are financed off balance sheet through special-purpose vehicles and private credit, and how banks pass the risk on, which is the mechanism behind this week's doubts about AI infrastructure valuations.

candidates.title: China is more exposed to semiconductor supply-chain disruptions than the US
candidates.why: Puts numbers under the 'chip war' talking point: Chinese demand needs about 2.7 times as much chip input per dollar as US demand, and in a Taiwan-plus-decoupling shock Chinese advanced processor prices rise roughly 17-fold against about 20 percent in the US.

candidates.title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
candidates.why: Cryo-electron microscopy finally captures the fleeting protein ring the malaria parasite uses to push its way into red blood cells, and the team used AI-assisted protein design to build an inhibitor that blocks it in the test tube: a new angle on a disease that kills about 600,000 people a year as drug resistance spreads.

candidates.title: How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls
candidates.why: A randomised experiment: 50 professional causal-inference analysts worked with a Claude agent whose lean on each analytical choice was set by coin flip. Analysts sided with the agent's lean 86 percent of the time and most echoed its arguments, yet few credited it. A clean piece of experimental design showing how an AI collaborator quietly steers expert conclusions, directly relevant to anyone doing analysis with agents.

candidates.title: Evolving Agent Teams
candidates.source: UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab (Cao, Mao, Li, Gonzalez, Stoica)
candidates.why: Single coding agents stall when writing hard GPU kernels: they abandon the difficult tensor-core route after a few failures and polish an easier, slower design. This paper has a supervisor agent diagnose each plateau and reorganise a team of agents (adding a profiler, a 'fresh eyes' role, a knowledge integrator). The result beats FlashInfer's hand-written production decode kernel for DeepSeek-style attention by 1.2x, and Kimi's attention kernels by over 3x. A concrete look at AI doing expert systems engineering, with the failure modes spelled out.

candidates.title: SGLang security update: improving request isolation
candidates.why: How Cloudflare's GLM-5.3 deployment leaked fragments of one user's conversation into another's output. Large models are now served by splitting each request across two machines, one reading the prompt and one writing the answer, with the first streaming its working memory into the second over the network. Writes already sent cannot be recalled, so a cancelled request can overwrite memory just handed to someone else. Explains why long-context AI serving makes this failure likely and how it was fixed.

candidates.title: AI can turn security fixes into working exploits before users receive an update
candidates.why: Epoch let an open-weight model, Z.ai's GLM 5.3, loose on Firefox security fixes that were already public in the source code but not yet shipped to users. Working alone for up to 48 hours with no internet, it built web pages that silently read and sent off a local file on six consecutive Firefox releases, at about 1,000 dollars of API spend per release, rediscovering an unpublished bug along the way; no provider refused a single request, while 100,000 dollars spent on Chrome failed. A first-hand, numbers-heavy look at how AI shrinks the window between a fix being published and attackers exploiting it.

candidates.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
candidates.why: Anthropic's science team reports seven concrete case studies of Claude inside drug development: CAR T-cell receptor designs 70 percent shorter that produced about ten times as many receptors in lab tests, 35,000 antibody designs against food allergies in a month, binders improved more than tenfold in ten weeks, regulatory document reviews cut from 25 hours to under three, and a one-person company that took a muscular dystrophy candidate to promising mouse results in under 18 months by coordinating 11 outside labs. A first-hand tour of AI changing what a small team can do in biotech, with real numbers; mostly preclinical, so the caveats matter.

candidates.title: How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle
candidates.why: Days before the US midterms, Quanta explains Condorcet's paradox (every voter consistent, the group going in circles) and Arrow's impossibility theorem through a picture: glue the six possible rankings of three candidates together edge by edge and you get a tube, and joining its ends with a twist turns it into a Klein bottle. Accessible topology with a concrete hook, showing why no voting rule can be fair in every sense at once.

candidates.title: Automated Subtle Emergent Misalignment Research
candidates.why: Anthropic's own account of setting Claude agents loose on a red-team task: write a few thousand fine-tuning examples that quietly make a small model misaligned while slipping past a data monitor. Every run eventually succeeded, mostly by hiding the bad behaviour inside fiction and role-play, which shows how automated research can find holes in training-data safeguards faster than people can, and why data filtering alone is a weak defence.

candidates.title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
candidates.source: Terence Tao's blog (guest post by Frank Calegari)
candidates.why: A leading number theorist's response to OpenAI's October release of more than 700 AI-written maths papers, which claimed solutions to famous open problems across whole fields. He compares the moment to the classification of finite simple groups, argues that choosing good problems and understanding proofs now matter more than producing them, and proposes concrete changes: judge every paper as if AI-assisted, interview candidates in person, demand more of journals or abandon them, and train students more broadly. A first-hand view of how AI is reshaping the economics of a whole research field.
candidates.who: Frank Calegari is a University of Chicago number theorist working on the Langlands programme, writing on Terence Tao's blog; he is an insider in exactly the fields the AI papers claim to have cracked.

candidates.title: The Disappearing Aid Check: The Future of US–Israel Defense Support
candidates.why: Trump said on 3 November that Israel's roughly 4 billion dollars a year in US military aid ends this year. This brief, by a former State Department and NSC official, explains what that aid actually is: the ten-year memorandum, Foreign Military Financing grants that Congress appropriates with strings attached, the share Israel may spend at home being phased out by 2028, and missile-defence money. Its central argument is that support will not vanish but move into Pentagon channels (procurement contracts, co-production, joint R&D) governed by acquisition rules with far less political oversight: 'quieter does not mean smaller'. Dense and policy-styled, and it argues a position, but it is the mechanism under today's headline.

candidates.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
candidates.why: Anthropic's own write-up of FlashProve, which lets a provider publish a fingerprint of a model's weights and then prove that a given reply came from exactly that model, without revealing the weights; anyone can check the proof on a CPU. It explains the goal (stopping a provider from quietly swapping in a cheaper model), the four guarantees a proof must give, and the engineering that made it practical: proving only the experts a mixture-of-experts model actually uses, batching proofs after the fact and streaming weights so it fits on one GPU. Real numbers throughout (about 72 times the GPU time of normal inference on Llama 4 Maverick, roughly 19 MB of proof per request, 17 seconds to verify), plus honest limits. The cryptographic machinery itself is named rather than explained, so read it for the what and why, not the proofs.

candidates.title: You don't need long context
candidates.why: NVIDIA researchers argue that the race to million-token context windows is largely unnecessary. They first show why long context is expensive: on popular open models, generating a token at 256K context costs 3.6 to 7 times more than at 16K, a gap hidden by flat per-token retail prices. Then they show that frontier models lose little or nothing on 13 long-horizon and long-input benchmarks when an agent keeps its working context short by summarising its state often and reading files selectively, and that a coding agent still works when it compacts after every single action. They end by proposing 'semantic state space models' that carry a plain-language state between steps. Both an inference-economics lesson and a provocative architectural claim.
